sutta: the mind. 27.2, "At Savatthi, the Buddha said, 'Monks, desire and lust for body is a corruption of the mind. Desire and lust for sounds, for odors, for tastes, for touch, for thoughts is a corruption of the mind. And a monk has abandoned abandoned the mental corruption in these six cases, his mind inclines to renunciation. The mind fortified by renunciation becomes wieldy in regard to those things that are to be realized by direct knowledge. Wieldy means easily used or controlled or handled. The mind fortified fortified by renunciation becomes easily controlled in regard to those things that are to be realized by direct knowledge. That means you can easily attain direct knowledge. So, desire and lust for the sense objects are a corruption of the mind. But when we abandon this uh we abandon this desire and lust for the six sense objects, then the mind is suitable to be used to realize direct knowledge. And the others are also quite similar. Desire and lust for the six sense bases, desire and lust for the six types of consciousness, for the contact or feeling, perception, volition, craving. And the next sutra I'll read now is the last one here, 27.10. Monks, the desire and lust for body, for feeling, for perception, for volition, for consciousness is a corruption of the mind. And among us abandoned the mental corruption in these five cases, his mind inclines to renunciation. The mind fortified by renunciation becomes wieldy in regard to those things that are to be realized by direct knowledge. So, here if a person has desire and lust for the five aggregates, then that is a corruption of the mind. But when he abandons the desire and lust for the five aggregates then the mind inclines renunciation and becomes very suitable to realize direct knowledge. Now we come to chapter 28. Sariputta Samyutta discourses concerning the venerable Sariputta.
